title: UK launch flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record-breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Flooding and drought are devolved areas for Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales but Defra says the devolved governments will still be part of the UK-wide taskforce, which will aim to bring together expertise and share information.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, gathering the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least £10.5bn until 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El Niño weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record.

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

Clarification 15 October: This article has been updated to explain that flooding and drought are devolved areas but that Defra has said devolved governments will still be part of the UK-wide taskforce.

title: Human-enhanced tsunami hazard in large lakes
author: Zafar
content:
The human footprint on Lake Iseo’s Delta

Lake Iseo (Italy) is located at the downstream end of Val Camonica (Fig. 1), one of the largest valleys of the southern European Alps. The Lake Iseo catchment (1777 km2) is characterized by steep topography and is drained by the Oglio River (Fig. 1), which inflows the lake from the north, supplying substantial sediment that forms a large delta. Extensive human activity in the catchment is well documented by archeological, historical, palynological, and paleoenvironmental studies32,33,34,35,36,37. Since the Roman period, intensified deforestation, agriculture, and pastoralism have significantly increased hillslope erosion, resulting in a threefold rise in sediment flux to the lake compared with earlier Holocene background levels32. This abrupt human-driven erosion rapidly built up and steepened the Oglio River Delta at the lake’s northern margin, overloading subaqueous slopes and increasing their susceptibility to collapse during seismic shaking17.

Fig. 1: Location and geomorphological context of Lake Iseo. Full size image a Location of the study area in the central Southern Alps, northern Italy. b Topographic map showing the Val Camonica watershed (black dashed line), along with the extent of Lake Iseo and adjacent basins, the locations of the main cities, and the epicenters of the 1117 and 1222 CE earthquakes. c The detailed bathymetry of Lake Iseo, showing the location of core SEB18 (core data in Supplementary Fig. 2), some of the seismic survey lines in white A–C (corresponding seismic profiles in Supplementary Fig. 1), the onshore core sites collected in this study, the Oglio River Delta, and the locations of the two medieval delta collapses.

The Val Camonica region has experienced moderate to high seismic activity due to the complex collisional and postcollisional phases of the Alpine orogeny38. Several destructive earthquakes have been recorded over the last two millennia39. Notably, two major medieval earthquakes, the 1117 CE Verona earthquake (Mw 6.5)39,40 and the 1222 CE Brescia earthquake (Mw 6.0)39,41, affected the Lake Iseo region, with estimated macroseismic intensities of approximately VI–VII42 and V–VI43, respectively. They triggered massive subaqueous delta collapses in Lake Iseo17 and induced minor slope failure, likely along the escarpment between Monte Isola and the eastern shore44. According to detailed sediment core and seismic reflection analyses, these delta collapses are recorded as the thickest mass-wasting deposits (MWDs, or megaturbidites) in the deep basin of Lake Iseo17. The 1117 CE earthquake produced an event deposit (MWD7 in Supplementary Fig. 1), which reached a maximum thickness of ~7 m and an estimated volume of \(6.2\,\times \,{10}^{7}{m}^{3}\) derived from the interpolated thickness (Fig. 2c). This exceptional event is linked to approximately six centuries of human-driven sediment accumulation at the Oglio River Delta following the last delta collapse in the 6th century (Supplementary Fig. 3)17. After the collapse of the 1117 CE, continued sedimentation from ongoing human activity rebuilt and preconditioned the delta slopes for another collapse, which occurred approximately one century later during the 1222 CE earthquake and produced a somewhat thinner layer (MWD6 in Supplementary Fig. 1) with a maximum thickness of ~2 m and a volume of \(1\times {10}^{7}\,{m}^{3}\) (Fig. 2f). This rapid rebuilding is supported by a first-order estimate based on the mean deep-basin sedimentation rate (~3 mm yr−1)17 over the ~18 km2 depositional area (below 210 m water depth), which indicates that ~5.7 Mm³ of sediment accumulated between the 1117 and 1222 CE events. Although it is lower than the ~10 Mm3 mobilized in 1222 CE, this estimate is conservative because it reflects fine-grained sediment preserved in the deep basin and does not include coarser sediment stored at the delta front, where the failure originated. The accommodation space created by the 1117 CE collapse likely further enhanced sediment trapping and rapid rebuilding of the unstable delta wedge. These two events illustrate how increases in sediment supply from human activities may amplify the likelihood of delta collapses in seismically active regions.

Fig. 2: Landslide modeling and its validation with geological records for the 1117 CE and 1222 CE events. Full size image a, d Initial reconstructed landslide volumes. b, e Simulated landslide thickness evolution over time. c, f Comparisons between modeled deposit thicknesses and those interpolated from seismic profiles are shown for the a–c 1117 CE event and d–f 1222 CE event. Background satellite imagery in (a, d): Google ©2026 CNES/Airbus, Maxar Technologies.

Reconstruction of catastrophic tsunami events

To assess the tsunami hazards associated with both medieval delta collapses, we reconstructed the landslides and resulting tsunamis by quantifying the event deposits and conducting high-resolution numerical modeling. The reconstruction was based on high-resolution LiDAR topographic and multibeam bathymetric datasets acquired in 2002 by Regione Lombardia and the Istituto Nazionale di Oceanografia e di Geofisica Sperimentale (OGS) within the Italian National Geological Mapping Program (CARG)45,46. The present-day high-resolution bathymetry was used as a geomorphological analogue for the pre-failure delta morphology because sustained sedimentation following the medieval failures largely infilled the delta front and obscured the original landslide scars. This was done assuming that continued sediment delivery after the medieval failures rebuilt the delta along a similar depositional pathway.

Based on this framework, the post-failure delta morphology was reconstructed in GIS by removing areas of sediment accumulation and restoring a plausible failure-scar morphology. This reconstruction was guided by large-scale bathymetric trends, erosional features, and the present-day morphology of the Oglio Delta front. Landslide source volumes were then estimated as the difference between the reconstructed post-failure surface and the modern bathymetric surface. The reconstruction was iteratively refined until the estimated source volumes matched the volumes of the mapped mass-wasting deposits identified from seismic reflection profiles and sediment-core data in the deep basin, yielding source volumes of 6.2 × 107 m3 for the 1117 CE event and 1.0 × 107 m3 for the 1222 CE event (Fig. 2a, d). We then simulated landslide dynamics using a viscoplastic rheological model assuming a single-event failure mechanism. This assumption is supported by the sedimentological structure of the deep-basin event deposits, which comprise an erosive sandy base interpreted as a high-energy remobilization phase, followed by a single upward-fining depositional episode without evidence for repeated grading or multiple stacked subevents17. This unit is overlain by thick homogeneous deposits interpreted as suspension settling associated with basin-wide seiche oscillations47, with an upper fine-clay interval representing the final stage of suspension settling.

Details of the modeling approach and parameter selection are provided in the Methods section. The temporal evolution of landslide thickness, from initiation to final deposition in the deep basin, is shown in Fig. 2b, e. Both landslides originated at the Oglio Delta, but their final depositional geometries differ slightly. During the 1222 CE event, a greater portion of the mass propagated farther into the basin compared to the 1117 CE event, likely due to greater accommodation space, as the 1117 CE deposits had already filled the northeastern deep basin with substantial sediment a century earlier. Moreover, the 1222 CE landslide had relatively high water content and a large proportion of coarse sediment (Supplementary Fig. 2), resulting in a relatively low shear strength. This allowed the material to travel more rapidly (Fig. 2e), with most of the sediment reaching farther into the deep basin. The modeled deposit thicknesses and their spatial distributions strongly agree with those inferred from seismic profiles and sediment core data for both events (Fig. 2c, f), thus validating the rheological assumption and parameterization of our landslide modeling approach.

Following this validation, we simulate the resulting tsunamis based on time-dependent changes in water depth induced by landslide motion. We calculated tsunami wave propagation and inundation by using a nonlinear hydrodynamic model for both events at a 10 m spatial resolution. Details of the tsunami models, Froude number estimation, and sensitivity analyses of dispersion and landslide initiation depth are provided in the Methods section. The maximum tsunami wave heights over the arrival times for both events, along with the corresponding run-up heights and inundation distances at the marked locations, are shown in Fig. 3. Our simulations reveal that the medieval delta collapses in Lake Iseo generated some of the largest subaquatic landslide-induced tsunamis ever inferred in a lacustrine setting. The 1117 CE event produced wave heights greater than 50 m in the northern part of the lake (Fig. 3a, c). This massive tsunami wave inundated nearby shores within just one minute and propagated up to ~2.7 km inland (Fig. 3d). The subsequent collapse in 1222 CE also generated a large tsunami (Fig. 3b), with waves peaking at ~13 m (Fig. 3c) and inundation extending up to ~1 km inland (Fig. 3d). Both tsunamis propagated rapidly across Lake Iseo and were strongly influenced by Monte Isola, the central island, which acts as a natural barrier, splitting the waves and partially shielding the cities behind it. Despite this protection, areas such as Iseo still experienced significant impacts, with maximum wave heights of ~5.5 m (1117 CE) and ~2 m (1222 CE), arriving ~7 min after the landslides (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3: Tsunami modeling and its coastal impact for the 1117 CE and 1222 CE events. Full size image Maximum tsunami surface elevation (colorbar) and wave arrival times in minutes (contour lines) for the a 1117 CE and b 1222 CE events. White dots indicate the municipalities surrounding Lake Iseo, and red dots indicate the onshore core sites collected in this study. c Run-up heights and d inundation distances at the sites marked in (a), ordered from north to south (N–S), for the 1117 CE (red) and 1222 CE (blue) events.

Historical and archeological tsunami evidence

Our numerical tsunami reconstructions are strongly supported by historical and archeological evidence. A vivid account from a 12th-century manuscript48 preserved in the Vatican Library describes the catastrophic 1117 CE event, which states on folio 184r: “Lacus quoque adeo excreverunt ut in villis iuxta positis habitantes paucissimi ab hoc periculo evaderent. Multa quoque castella et arces cum interitu habitantium miserabiliter diruerunt.” meaning, “The lake (Iseo) overflowed so much that very few of the inhabitants of the nearby villages escaped this danger. Many castles and fortresses also collapsed miserably, with the destruction of their inhabitants”. Detailed information on individual buildings is limited, making it difficult to validate the exact tsunami run-up and inundation. However, archeological evidence from the Pieve church of Sant’Andrea d’Iseo provides useful constraints46. The church underwent major reconstruction shortly after the 1117 CE event, involving both its lower and upper parts. Whether this damage resulted from seismic shaking, tsunami impact, or both cannot be determined. Our simulations indicate that the 1117 CE tsunami reached the shoreline in front of the church with a maximum wave height of ~3.5 m and an inundation distance of 165 m, sufficient to inundate the church area.

Additionally, archeological investigations have documented extensive structural damage around Lake Iseo’s shore following the 1222 CE earthquake49, supporting the occurrence of another important tsunami event. Together, these historical and archeological pieces of evidence for both events strongly support our comprehensive numerical reconstruction, confirming that delta collapses triggered two exceptionally large catastrophic tsunamis in Lake Iseo over a century apart.

We also investigated the potential preservation of tsunami deposits along Lake Iseo’s shoreline. However, extensive human modification has largely erased natural sedimentary archives. The only remaining undisturbed site, a peatland at the southern tip near Iseo, was cored at multiple locations using a Russian corer. Numerical models, however, indicate minimal wave heights (<1 m) at this site (Fig. 3) due to wave diffraction around Monte Isola, which splits incoming waves, resulting in indirect and attenuated wave propagation toward the southern tip. Consequently, no identifiable tsunami deposits were found at this site, which is consistent with the findings of Zafar et al.50, highlighting the importance of wave height and directivity in controlling the spatial distribution of tsunami deposits along lake shores. Other factors, such as localized sedimentation dynamics, erosion, historical peatland exploitation or undocumented disturbances, may also explain the apparent absence of deposits on land.

title: Severe drought declared in parts of southern England
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
South East Water's operations director Douglas Whitfield said standpipes remained part of the company's drought plan but were unlikely to be needed.

Whitfield said a wet winter had been forecast but timings were not clear and the firm was making any adjustments it could to protect supplies.

Whitfield said South East Water, which supplies more than two million customers, said 92 repair crews were out across Sussex and Kent tackling leaks to minimise loss from the network.

In an email sent to customers South East Water said it was optimising water pressure across the county and had more than doubled the number of teams tackling leaks in the region, increasing from seven to 16.

It said the number of leaks in the affected area had fallen from 181 to 97 and that more than 1,300 leaks had been repaired since 1 April.

Wessex Water, which supplies customers from Wimbleball, introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years in August and said the restrictions would remain in place for the foreseeable future.

The water company said it had increased leak repairs, moved water into the area from more resilient sources and adjusted water pressure in some communities to conserve supplies and urged customers to continue using water carefully.

Will Willoughby, director of water supply at Wessex Water, said: "We saw record levels of demand through the network - and it sustained above the 400 million litres a day for 48 days, which is far and away the toughest year that we've seen in terms of that height in demand."

He said customer impact "should be none" but encouraged customers to continue to be mindful about water usage.

Paul Tompkins, deputy president of The National Farmers' Union (NFU) said it had been a "torrid year for farmers", where the conditions proved "very difficult" to harvest crops, provide water for livestock, and a "potential dry winter could have implications for next year's crops".

title: Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone
author: Adam Burke
content:
Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Department

Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding.

The adjoining states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona all saw substantial flooding last week, and damage assessments are just starting to trickle in from cities, towns and some of the most remote territory in the continental U.S.

The northern New Mexico city of Farmington was hit particularly hard after torrential rains fell on the San Juan mountains in Colorado, sending floodwaters down the San Juan River that passes through Farmington on its way to Lake Powell on the Utah-Arizona border.

San Juan River saw some of biggest surges

Small towns all along the river, from Pagosa Springs, Colorado, to Bloomfield, New Mexico and Bluff, Utah all saw historic flooding and are now assessing recovery challenges.

About 46,000 people live in Farmington, long a center for coal, oil and natural gas production. It's also an important hub for the northeast side of the Navajo reservation, which sprawls across three states.

Sponsor Message

Farmington residents started getting evacuation notices on their phones as early as Wednesday night.

"My sister was notified on Thursday that she had to get out," said Connie Gooch, who has lived in Farmington for more than 65 years.

Gooch's sister owns a house in a suburban neighborhood near the San Juan River.

"Every year she goes through this," Gooch said. "The river starts rising, and she starts making sandbags to put around. But this year it was so fast she didn't have time to do that."

toggle caption i San Juan County Office of Emergency Management

According to National Weather Service data from a river gauge in Farmington, the San Juan grew 13 times larger in just 36 hours, late last week.

In the wee hours of Thursday morning, the river was about 3.5 feet high. By Friday, it was 14 feet high, flooding neighborhoods across the city, and possibly setting a record for the highest water ever recorded in the city.

This even after the Navajo Reservoir upstream from Farmington was able to mostly contain water rushing down from the mountains. But downstream of the reservoir, flood surges into the city came from two normally dry tributaries, Gobernador Canyon and Cañon Largo.

"This is a catastrophic flood of historic proportions," said Devon Neeley, San Juan County's public information officer.

Sponsor Message

"This river got wider than we have ever seen it in our lifetimes."

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Department

From Colorado peaks to Arizona deserts

Similar reports are coming in from the other side of the San Juan mountains in Colorado.

"It's nothing like most of us have seen before," said Tyler Schmidt, captain of the fire and rescue team in the small town of South Fork, Colo. on the banks of the Rio Grande. "We had several neighborhoods that were under two to three feet of water."

Colorado Public Radio's Dan Boyce reports that responders' immediate priorities are lifting final evacuation orders as waters recede. Damaged bridges need to be assessed. Well water all down the Rio Grande's path in the San Luis valley needs to be tested.

Other drinking water impacts from the storm include sewage spills from flooded treatment plants in Sedona, Arizona and other locations. KNAU reports extensive damage on the Hopi reservation.

The Hopi reservation is surrounded by the Navajo reservation, where there have also been reports of rescues, washed out roads and flooding of historic proportions.

San Juan County, New Mexico's Neeley said fire crews, police officers, National Guard troops, and even out-of-state swift water teams rescued between 200 and 300 county residents.

"We have pulled people out of vehicles stuck in running washes. We have pulled people by helicopter off of rooftops," Neeley said. "We have used not only high-clearance vehicles from the National Guard, but amphibious vehicles because the water is so high. It's been a lot."

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Deparment

Some relief in the works

By Sunday, the rain had eased, river levels were falling, and some residents started returning home to assess flood damage.

Connie Gooch delivered tarps and other materials to her sister's house.

"The river was up four feet in her house," she said.

She found a neighborhood full of people moving furniture out of their homes and piling demolition debris in their front yards.

Sponsor Message

"There were trucks and cars all over the place," Gooch said. "There was a guy in front of me carrying a loaded trailer full of sheet rock that they'd chipped out of somebody's house."

But officials want the thousands of evacuated residents to stay out for now.

"The public is anxious to get back in; we recognize that, we're sympathetic to that," said San Juan County Fire Chief David Vega at a public briefing Sunday. "Now that the swift water component is out of the way, that exposes a whole new set of hazards for us," Vega added.

Public officials are concerned about hazards like raw sewage and damaged gas lines, live power lines, and the floodwater itself.

"The water is not healthy," Vega said. "Stay out of the water. Gas, diesel, pesticides, fertilizer, these are not things that you want on your clothes."

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Deparment

New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham visited San Juan County on Monday.

Grisham said that the damage to infrastructure alone could cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

"I hope we're only spending 30 to 40 million (dollars)," Lujan Grisham said, responding to recovery cost estimates from San Juan County manager Mike Stark.

"We think this could be closer to between 200 and 300 million (dollars)," Lujan Grisham said. "The environmental issues and the road issues and infrastructure issues alone, really are expensive."

Monday night, Governor Lujan Grisham released an announcement, stating that the federal government has "partially granted" New Mexico's request for an emergency declaration in response to the regional flooding. Yesterday, Lujan-Grisham signed executive orders making $8.25 million more in state funding available for flood response.

title: How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias
author: Willa Rubin
content:
How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias

toggle caption i RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images

Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, is expected to make landfall on Friday evening near the Alabama Gulf Coast and Florida panhandle.

Days ago, the oil industry around the U.S. Gulf Coast started preparing. A segment of the nation's oil infrastructure — like oil rigs and platforms — operates in the region, although the majority of it is further west, towards western Louisiana and Texas.

Although oil experts are not anticipating major disruptions, oil companies have been taking precautions. Shell and BP have evacuated personnel from offshore facilities close to the storm's path, mainly deepwater platforms. Chevron has evacuated offshore drilling rigs close to the storm's path, and plans to redeploy them once the storm has passed.

Sponsor Message

In an emailed statement, Exxon told NPR they are "closely monitoring the weather. Operations are normal."

But so far, the storm seems like it will skirt most facilities. The storm's path "could be worse," said Debnil Chowdhury, head of Americas refining at S&P Global Energy. After all, the storm is heading east, and not west, toward where the bulk of oil operations — like refineries — are located.

The storm is "making a swooping turn, almost just to the east of where the most significant infrastructure is," said Bryan Domangue, the Gulf of America region director for the federal Marine Minerals Administration, who oversees offshore oil and natural gas production. "At this point, it's swept just a little south of some of our major deepwater oil and gas facilities, and then it's hugging the eastern boundary of where the infrastructure is."

He added that in addition to evacuating people who work on oil rigs and platforms, which are normal storm precautions, oil operators are doing things like shutting off safety valves below the ocean floor, and moving mobile drilling facilities when possible.

Of course, it's not unprecedented for the oil industry to face hurricanes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita , in 2005, remain some of the most destructive in the oil and gas industry's history. Nearly 3,000 platforms were in the path of the storms and Katrina destroyed 47 platforms. Other, more recent, hurricanes have not been as destructive but have halted production or reduced capacity — such as Hurricane Francine in 2024 , Hurricane Ida in 2021 , and Hurricane Harvey in 2017 .

Sponsor Message

Another risk is what would happen if the storm became severe enough to make refineries — which are on land — go offline, analysts told NPR. If a hurricane knocks out the power, or if a refinery floods, it can take a while to get running again. It's more complicated than restarting an oil rig or mobile drilling operations.

"Restarting these things is like starting up an old car," said Carl Larry, a manager at Enverus, an energy data and research provider, even if the shutdown is short. "If you did anything in the world, anything in your life, 24/7, stop doing it for one day," he continued, "you're going to have the shakes."

He says, this is because refineries are vast and complex. They boil oil down into molecules that are turned into diesel, gasoline, or natural gas liquids like propane. Pipelines carry crude oil in and refined products out. And they have to be heated. "Every one of those little steps is built on power that's generated through the facility on a constant 24/7 basis," Larry said. If that power is switched off, the process takes time to restart.

There are two significant refineries on the hurricane's path — the Chevron Pascagoula location and the Vertex Alabama refinery. Representatives of these refineries did not return requests for comment about their storm preparations, but Ross Allen, a spokesperson for Chevron, told NPR that generally speaking, refineries prepare for storms by trying to mitigate flood risk.

Chowdhury of S&P Global Energy said these two refineries "account for about 2.5% of total U.S. refining capacity and about 5% the Gulf Coast refining capacity. And Pascagoula specifically is very important to supplying airports throughout the southeast."

While those numbers may not sound big, the global supply of diesel and gas is short, due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. So every little bit counts. American refineries are operating at 92.7% capacity, refining about 17 million barrels of crude a day.

title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
author: Watch Our Pick Of Standout Clips Across The Bbc
content:
Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in Penonomé collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.

Another video showed a local hotel had almost completely collapsed.

Ricardo Brown, who lives in the southern Herrera province, told news agency Reuters that the earthquake had damaged several homes in his neighbourhood of Las Minas.

"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked and we're afraid it could fall on us," the 74-year-old said.

The full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, though several large aftershocks were also reported near the initial earthquake, potentially complicating the situation on the surface.

The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.

Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, and were seen taking to the streets or sitting in nearby parks until the shaking had ceased.

Damage in the capital appears to be limited to that caused by debris falling from roofs.

Panama's President José Raúl Mulino said his entire government was mobilising in response to the earthquake, adding: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."
